scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

axes.name: Property Form
axes.negPole: Full Communism / To Each by Need

questions.text: Small groups of trusted comrades acting on shared affinity are a more honest basis for organising than any mass structure.
Formal, large-membership organisations tend to develop the very hierarchies anarchists are trying to abolish.
An affinity group can move faster and stay truer to its principles than a mass union ever could.
Informal networks of relationships are a more resilient basis for revolutionary organising than any formal structure.
The intimacy of a small group protects against the bureaucratic drift that larger organisations can't avoid.
Building loose, overlapping networks beats building one large durable organisation.
A mass union rooted in the workplace is the only vehicle with the numbers to actually confront capital.
Organising has to scale to the size of the working class, which means building large membership structures.
Small affinity groups can be principled, but they will never have the leverage a mass organisation has.
The union floor, not the affinity group, is where most workers actually encounter anarchist ideas.
Durable mass organisation, not informal networking, is what turns sympathy into a movement.
A revolutionary union federation can mobilise numbers that no network of small groups can match.
An anarchist organisation should unite around a single strategic programme that binds every member.
Collective responsibility for the organisation's decisions is a serious commitment members should be held to.
A federation that tolerates real disagreement over strategy and ideology among its affiliates ends up capable of nothing.
Tactical unity across an organisation matters more than accommodating every internal disagreement.
An organisation strong enough to act needs agreed positions its members are expected to defend.
Programmatic coherence is what let some anarchist organisations act decisively where looser ones couldn't.
A federation should be a loose space where different anarchist tendencies coexist without a single binding programme.
Requiring ideological and tactical unity narrows a federation into a sect.
Anarchist organisation should preserve the autonomy of each group and current within it, not override it.
A synthesis of communists, syndicalists, and individualists in one federation is a strength, not a weakness.
Binding collective responsibility on individual members contradicts anarchism's basic commitments.
The looser the federation, the more genuinely anarchist its internal life remains.
Goods should be distributed according to need, with no accounting of what any individual contributed.
Money and exchange between individuals should be abolished, not merely redistributed more fairly.
Even labour itself should not be measured or exchanged once scarcity is overcome.
Full communism, not mutual exchange, is the goal a genuinely free society should aim at.
Once production is collectivised, the next step is abolishing exchange between individuals altogether.
A free society has no need to track who produced what.
Individuals should hold and freely exchange the product of their own labour rather than pool it into a common stock.
Mutual credit between free associations of producers is a fairer basis for exchange than pooling everything in common.
Possession of what one uses and produces is legitimate; ownership of what one doesn't is not.
A market of small producers exchanging freely, without capital or usury, is compatible with anarchism.
Even under anarchism, some form of accounting for individual contribution is fair and necessary.
Occupancy and use, not communal pooling, should determine who controls a given piece of land or tool.
Violence in self-defence and in overthrowing an oppressive order is legitimate.
Expropriating capital by force is a justifiable revolutionary act.
Waiting for a purely peaceful transition means waiting forever, since the state will not surrender its violence voluntarily.
Armed defence of a popular uprising against counter-revolution is not a betrayal of anarchist principles.
There is nothing inconsistent about anarchists organising armed resistance when the situation demands it.
A revolution that refuses all force will be crushed by a state that has none of the same scruples.
Anarchism should commit to nonviolence as a matter of consistent principle, not just tactics.
Using violence to achieve a stateless society reproduces the domination it claims to abolish.
Means and ends can't be separated; a violent revolution will produce a violent aftermath.
Nonviolent resistance and mutual aid do more to build a free society than armed struggle does.
Anarchists who take up arms end up organised like the states they oppose.
Coercion of any kind, even in a revolutionary cause, contradicts anarchism's basic commitments.
Modern industry and technology can be reorganised for collective benefit rather than rejected outright.
Large-scale infrastructure and coordination are compatible with a stateless, classless society.
Rejecting industrial technology altogether would condemn most people to a much harder life than they need to live.
Technology is a tool whose effects depend on who controls it, not something inherently opposed to freedom.
A federated, technologically advanced society is a realistic goal, not a contradiction in terms.
Anarchists should aim to seize and repurpose industrial capacity, not dismantle it.
Civilisation itself — mass society, agriculture, division of labour — is the root of domination, not just its capitalist form.
A genuinely free life means abandoning industrial technology and its dependencies, not redistributing them.
Complex technological systems require the very hierarchy and expertise anarchists are trying to abolish.
Returning to small-scale, low-technology ways of living is the only way to actually end domination.
Mass society and its infrastructure cannot be organised without reproducing coercive control.
The domestication of nature that founded civilisation is itself the first act of domination.
Building cooperatives, communes, and mutual aid networks now is how the new society is actually constructed.
A revolution has to prefigure the world it wants; the means must already resemble the ends.
Creating working alternative institutions matters as much as tearing down the existing ones.
Practising self-management now, on however small a scale, is real revolutionary work.
Counter-institutions built before the revolution give people something to defend and expand once it comes.
A movement that never builds anything concrete has nothing to offer once the old order falls.
The task is disruption and rupture; blueprints for a future society are premature and constraining.
Building alternative institutions can become an accommodation with the existing order rather than a threat to it.
No amount of prefigurative organising substitutes for actually destroying the systems of domination.
Cooperatives and communes that operate within capitalism end up managing themselves under its rules, not escaping them.
Rupture has to come before construction; you cannot build the new world inside the shell of the old.
Focusing energy on alternative institutions can dull the urgency of confronting power directly.
Confederations of directly democratic municipal assemblies are a viable form of anarchist self-government.
Local assemblies, federated upward, can perform the coordinating functions anarchists need without becoming a state.
A directly democratic municipality is not a government in the sense anarchists oppose.
Citizens' assemblies claiming legitimate public power can be a real transitional strategy toward a stateless society.
Running candidates for local office on a libertarian municipalist platform is a defensible anarchist tactic.
Dual power built through confederated municipalities is a credible path beyond the nation-state.
Any structure claiming to exercise public, binding authority — even a local assembly — is a government and should be rejected.
Federating assemblies from the ground up still recreates layers of representation anarchists should refuse.
There is no such thing as a legitimate government, local or confederal, direct or representative.
Anarchism means the negation of the state as such, not its replacement with a smaller, friendlier version.
Running for local office, however framed, concedes the legitimacy of electoral government.
A confederation with binding votes across municipalities is still a form of rule over the minority.
Gender, race, and sexuality are independent axes of domination that class struggle alone does not explain or resolve.
A movement that centres only class will reproduce patriarchal and racial hierarchies within itself.
Confronting patriarchy and white supremacy is as fundamental to anarchism as confronting capital and the state.
Domination takes many forms that don't reduce to economic exploitation.
Anarchist organising has to actively centre those most marginalised, not treat their oppression as secondary.
The abolition of the state and capital does not automatically abolish patriarchy or racial hierarchy.
Class exploitation is the foundation that other forms of domination ultimately rest on.
Once capitalism and the state are abolished, the material basis for other hierarchies falls away with them.
Organising around identity fragments the working class instead of uniting it against its common enemy.
Class struggle is what actually unites people across the divisions capital uses to keep them apart.
Prioritising any single axis of oppression other than class ends up serving capital by dividing its opponents.
The point of production remains the central site of struggle, whatever other hierarchies also exist.
